newsitem.title: RWANDA: Only few Canadians in Zaire "multinational" force.
newsitem.headline: Only few Canadians in Zaire "multinational" force.

text.p: More than two weeks after the U.N. Security Council launched a multinational force to save refugees in Zaire, a mere 200 or so Canadians have arrived in the region but are still hundreds of miles from where food is needed.
A spokesman for the Canadian-led force said on Tuesday that 206 Canadians were in place at the force's headquarters at Entebbe airport on the shores of Lake Victoria in Uganda.
"It's a gradual buildup. I don't know how many Hercules flights are arriving every day," said Major Rod Babuik, spokesman for the liaison unit in the Rwandan capital Kigali.
The forces include a command centre, a surgical team and a detachment of transport planes which could drop food for the hundreds of thousands of refugees, he added.
Forty-nine personnel are on standby at Stuttgart in Germany, the force's rear headquarters, and 424 more are on 24 hours' notice to deploy to Uganda from Ontario and Alberta in Canada.
But the force is yet to start reconnaisance flights over eastern Zaire and the foot patrols announced by force commander Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril last week have been delayed.
"We haven't got all the approvals necessary to conduct the reconnaisance into Zaire and we are meeting with Rwandan officials today," Babiuk said.
"It's frustrating, but to avoid a dangerous situation it is important to make sure you have all the necessary approvals before going in," Babiuk said.
Babiuk was unable to say when other nations slated to join the Canadians would start arriving at Entebbe. The U.N. Security Council gave its approval to the force on November 15.

In the last three week, plans for the international force have been reduced from a proposed 15,000-member military force in eastern Zaire to a logistical team based in Uganda to see if relief can be airdropped, a plan criticised as ineffective by aid agencies.

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said on Monday that hundreds of thousands of men, women and children were still facing hunger, disease and violent death, most of them scattered in inaccessible and inhospitable areas of eastern Zaire.
More than 20 countries, including the United States, France, Britain, Belgium, Senegal and South Africa, were expected to contribute to the force.
Independently, U.S. and British reconnaisance planes have made sorties over rebel-held eastern Zaire in search of hundreds of thousands of missing refugees.
British defence sources said they believed it unlikely that a large-scale multinational force would be needed because a reconnaissance mission found far fewer refugees than expected.
The British aerial mission over eastern Zaire located only around 200,000 refugees and displaced people, compared with the 700,000 estimated by the United Nations' refugee agency.
The refugees are mainly Rwandans and Burundians who fled eastern border camps in October and November because of fighting between the army and ethnic Tutsi Zairean rebels.
They include some of the Rwandan Hutu militiamen responsible for killing up to one million people in Rwanda during the genocide of 1994.
Around 500,000 refugees returned to Rwanda from Goma camps between November 15 and 19.
Rwanda refuses to allow the multinational force to use its territory as a base, arguing that most refugees have gone back home. The force has failed to obtain permission to overfly or enter Zaire.
The Zairean government opposes airdrops of food while the rebels who control much of eastern Zaire do not want the multinational force to deploy in large numbers in their area.
As a result the Canadian air force has confined its operations to flying medical aid to refugees in Tanzania, while acknowledging this is not their main mission.
